area.name: Around the house
area.blurb: Everyday home fixes and safety checks for power, water, air, alarms, and walls, plus the science behind them.
area.intro: These guides cover the small jobs and safety checks that keep a home running: resetting power, shutting off water, fixing a running toilet, clearing clogs, changing the furnace filter, testing alarms, and simple wall repairs. Each one also explains the science or math behind the job, from watts and amps to water pressure and buoyancy. The electrical guides stick to what homeowners commonly do safely, like resetting and testing; anything involving wiring belongs to a licensed electrician.

deeper.label: The Trades
deeper.text: Ready for more? Full courses on plumbing, electrical, HVAC and construction: how every part of a house works, how the parts fit together, how to troubleshoot by symptom, and which jobs to leave to licensed pros.

guides.name: Reset a Tripped Circuit Breaker
guides.time: about 10 minutes (about an hour to label a whole panel)
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: When part of your home suddenly loses power, a circuit breaker has often switched itself off to protect the wiring. Knowing where your breaker panel is, how to reset a breaker, and which breaker runs which room saves time in the dark. This guide is for U.S.-style breaker panels and covers only the switches a homeowner is meant to use.
need: Pen and paper, or the label card inside the panel door
before: If you see sparks, hear sizzling or buzzing, or smell something burning, don't go near the panel. Call the fire department right away.
If the panel is wet, or you can see any wires, don't touch it. Call a licensed electrician.
Turn off the lights and unplug appliances in the rooms that lost power.

steps.how: Walk around and note which lights and outlets stopped working. Turn off the light switches and unplug appliances in those rooms, so nothing switches on the moment power comes back.
In many homes, especially older ones, the panel is in a garage or a storage closet. Some homes have more than one panel, inside or outside.
Open the panel door. Breakers are rows of small switches. A tripped one sits all the way at OFF or stuck partway between ON and OFF.
Stand a little to the side of the panel. Using one hand, push the tripped handle firmly all the way to OFF.
Now push the handle firmly to ON. Close the panel door.
See if the lights and outlets work again. Plug things back in one at a time, and spread big power users across different circuits instead of running them all on one.
If the breaker trips again right away, or you can't figure out why it tripped, leave it OFF and call a licensed electrician.

On a calm day, with a helper, switch off one breaker at a time and note which lights and outlets go dark. Write the rooms on the panel's label card. Warn everyone first, since clocks and computers will lose power.
Show everyone in the household where the panel is and what a tripped breaker looks like.

pro: Call a licensed electrician if a breaker trips again right after you reset it or keeps tripping.
Call an electrician instead of resetting if the panel is wet, you can see wires, or more than one breaker has tripped.
Call a licensed electrician soon if lights dim or flicker, or if outlets, switches, plugs, or cords feel unusually warm.
If you see sparks, hear sizzling or buzzing, or smell something burning, call the fire department right away.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why a breaker trips
body: Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a wire, measured in amps. Voltage is the push that moves the current, measured in volts. In standard U.S. homes, regular outlets supply 120 volts.

Power, measured in watts, tells how fast a device uses energy. You find it by multiplying volts by amps. Each breaker protects one circuit and allows only a set number of amps. If more current flows than that, the wires could get too hot, so the breaker switches itself off. That's called tripping.

Here is the math for a 15-amp circuit: 120 volts × 15 amps = 1,800 watts. Say your space heater's label says 1,500 watts and your microwave's label says 1,000 watts. Together that's 2,500 watts. Divide by 120 volts and you get about 21 amps, which is more than 15. Click: the breaker trips.
how_it_works.formula: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts)
how_it_works.try: With an adult, find the labels on three unplugged appliances, like a lamp, a toaster, and a hair dryer. Write down each one's watts and divide by 120 to estimate its amps. Which two together would go over 15 amps?

teach: Visit the panel together in daylight, long before you ever need it.
Let your child hold the flashlight and find the tripped switch while you reset it.
Make labeling a team project: one person flips breakers, the other walks around and reports what went dark.
Turn appliance labels into a math game with the watts formula.
tips: Keep a flashlight near the panel.
Write down each time a breaker trips and what was running. A pattern helps an electrician find the cause.
Extension cords and power strips are for temporary use only.
Don't run a space heater on a light-duty extension cord. It can't carry that much current.

mistakes.problem: Resetting the same breaker over and over.
mistakes.fix: A breaker that keeps tripping is a warning sign. Leave it off and call a licensed electrician.

mistakes.problem: Pushing a tripped handle straight to ON, and nothing happens.
mistakes.fix: Push it firmly all the way to OFF first, then to ON.

mistakes.problem: Running a space heater and a microwave on the same circuit.
mistakes.fix: Spread high-wattage appliances across different circuits.

mistakes.problem: A panel with no labels, so you guess in the dark.
mistakes.fix: Map and label every breaker now, while the power is on and nothing is wrong.

safety: Never touch a panel that is wet. Call an electrician.
If you can see any wires in the panel, stop and call an electrician.
Use extension cords and power strips only for temporary needs.

guides.name: Test and Reset a GFCI Outlet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 10.
guides.intro: A GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter) outlet is the kind with TEST and RESET buttons, usually found near water in kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and outdoors. It cuts the power in a split second when electricity starts leaking where it shouldn't, such as through water or a person. Testing it once a month tells you it still works, and knowing how to reset it can bring a 'dead' outlet back to life.
need: A small lamp or night-light that you know works
Paper and pencil (to note which outlets each GFCI controls)
before: If the GFCI has tripped, unplug whatever was running on it and check the cord for fraying or other damage.

steps.how: Look for outlets with TEST and RESET buttons in bathrooms, the kitchen, the garage, the basement or crawl space, laundry and utility sinks, and outdoors. Some homes have GFCI breakers in the panel instead, with a TEST button on the breaker.
Plug a lamp or night-light into the GFCI outlet and turn it on. If it doesn't light, press RESET first.
Push the TEST button. The light should go out. On a GFCI breaker, pressing TEST should move the handle to the tripped position.
Push RESET firmly. The light should come back on. For a GFCI breaker, reset the handle.
A GFCI outlet also protects the outlets wired after it on the same circuit. Next time you test, check which other outlets lose power and write them down.
If a regular outlet stops working, look for a tripped GFCI on the same circuit, which may be in another room. Unplug what was running, then press RESET.
If the light stays on when you press TEST, or won't come back on after RESET, the GFCI is not doing its job. Have a qualified electrician fix or replace it.
Test each GFCI once a month and after a power outage.

pro: If the light stays on when you press TEST, the GFCI isn't working or isn't installed right. Have a qualified electrician correct it.
If RESET won't bring the power back, the GFCI needs to be replaced. Replacing it is wiring work, so have a qualified electrician do it.
If a GFCI keeps tripping, or you can't tell why it tripped, contact an electrician.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: How a GFCI notices a leak
body: Electricity travels in a loop. Current flows out to your lamp on one wire and comes back on another. In a healthy circuit, the amount going out equals the amount coming back.

A GFCI keeps comparing those two amounts. If some current is missing on the way back, it must be leaking out another path, maybe through water or a person. When the difference reaches just a few thousandths of an amp, about 4 to 6 milliamps, the GFCI shuts off the power in less than a tenth of a second.
A milliamp is one-thousandth of an amp. That means a GFCI can notice a leak far smaller than the current a lamp uses, and act on it faster than you can blink.
how_it_works.formula: leak = current out − current back; the GFCI trips when the leak reaches about 0.004 to 0.006 amps (4 to 6 milliamps)
how_it_works.try: Math warm-up: 1 amp = 1,000 milliamps. If a lamp uses 0.5 amps, how many milliamps is that? (500.) How many times bigger is that than a 5-milliamp leak? (100 times.)

teach: Make testing a first-of-the-month family routine.
Let your child press TEST and RESET while you both watch the lamp.
Draw a simple house map together showing which outlets go dark when each GFCI trips.
tips: Use a lamp you can see from the outlet so you know right away when it goes off.
Test after every power outage too.
If a GFCI trips every time one certain appliance is plugged in, that appliance may be faulty. Stop using it.
For outdoor power tools and electric garden equipment, use portable GFCI protection.

mistakes.problem: Deciding an outlet is broken when it's really fed by a tripped GFCI somewhere else.
mistakes.fix: Check the GFCI outlets in nearby bathrooms, the kitchen, garage, basement, and outside, and press RESET.

mistakes.problem: Never testing because the outlet 'works fine'.
mistakes.fix: A GFCI can stop protecting you and still deliver power. In one CPSC survey, about a quarter of people who tested their GFCIs found one that wasn't working. Test monthly.

mistakes.problem: Pressing RESET over and over on a GFCI that keeps tripping.
mistakes.fix: Unplug everything on it. If it still trips, or you can't tell why, call an electrician.

safety: If TEST doesn't cut the power, don't count on that outlet for protection until a qualified electrician fixes it.

guides.name: Shut Off Your Home's Water
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: When a pipe bursts or a sink overflows, every minute of running water adds to the damage. Your home has a main shutoff valve that stops water to the whole house, and most sinks and toilets have their own small valves. Find them now, before you need them.
need: A tag or tape and a marker, for labeling
A water key or wrench, only if your main valve needs one
before: Learn where the main valve is now, before there's a leak.
Leave the valve at the water meter or property line alone. For that one, call your water utility or a licensed plumber.

steps.t: Look where the water comes in
steps.how: The main valve is usually close to where the water line enters the house. In a basement, check the front wall facing the street, typically within 3 to 5 feet of where the pipe comes in. In a home without a basement, look near the water heater or under the kitchen sink. Some are on an outside wall or in an underground box.
A round wheel handle closes by turning clockwise, and it may take two or more full turns. A lever handle closes with a quarter turn; it's off when the lever sits crossways to the pipe.
Turn the handle to closed with steady pressure. If it's rusted, stuck, or won't close all the way, plan to have a licensed plumber repair or replace it.
Open a faucet on the highest floor. This lets out the leftover pressure. The water should slow and stop. If it keeps flowing, the valve isn't closing fully.
Open a wheel valve about half a turn, or a lever about halfway, so the pipes fill gently. Then open it all the way and let each faucet run until the sputtering air stops.

Look under sinks and behind toilets for small valves on the water lines. A toilet's valve is usually on the wall behind it and closes clockwise. These let you shut off one fixture and keep water running everywhere else.
Tag the main valve so it's easy to spot. Show everyone in the family where it is and how to turn it.

pro: If your home has no main valve, or it's rusted, stuck, or won't shut off completely, have a licensed plumber repair or replace it.
For the valve at the meter or property line, call your water utility or a licensed plumber.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Water pressure and the one way in
body: The water in your pipes is under pressure. Pressure is a force spread over an area, measured in pounds per square inch (psi). Many homeowners set their house pressure to around 50 psi. A widely used plumbing code calls for a pressure regulator, a valve that lowers the pressure, when the supply pressure is over 80 psi.

Where does the push come from? Water systems use pumps, and water stored up high in tanks. Each foot of water height adds about 0.433 psi at the bottom. So if the water's surface sits 115 feet above your faucet, it pushes with about 115 × 0.433, which is close to 50 psi.

That pressure fills every pipe in your house at once. But all of it comes in through one service line, and the main valve sits on that line. Close it, and no new water can get in. Open a faucet to let out the leftover pressure, and the flow stops everywhere downstream.
how_it_works.try: Use the formula: how tall would a water tower need to be to give 60 psi? (60 ÷ 0.433 ≈ 139 feet.) Next time you pass a water tower, guess how tall it is and estimate the pressure it makes.

teach: Go on a valve hunt together: the main valve first, then every sink and toilet.
Let your child practice closing and opening a fixture valve while you watch.
Play 'what would you do?': 'Water is spraying under the bathroom sink. What do you turn first?'
tips: If a pipe breaks or bursts, close the main valve right away. The faster the water is off, the less damage it can do.
Check the main valve now and then to make sure it isn't rusty and still closes completely.
If your home has fire sprinklers, there may be two valves. Unless a sprinkler pipe is the one leaking, close only the household plumbing valve and leave the sprinkler pipes on.
Keep a flashlight near the main valve.

mistakes.problem: Hunting for the valve while water pours in.
mistakes.fix: Find it and tag it today.

mistakes.problem: Turning a lever handle around and around like a wheel.
mistakes.fix: A lever only needs a quarter turn. It's off when it points across the pipe.

mistakes.problem: Opening the main valve all the way at once after a repair.
mistakes.fix: Open it partway, let the pipes fill, then open it fully and let the air out of the faucets.

mistakes.problem: Using the valve at the meter or curb.
mistakes.fix: Use your home's own main valve. Call the water utility or a licensed plumber for the one at the meter.

safety: Don't operate the valve at the meter or property line yourself. Call your water utility or a licensed plumber.

guides.name: Fix a Running Toilet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A toilet that keeps running, or refills on its own, is quietly pouring water and money down the drain. A worn flapper alone can silently leak thousands of gallons a year. Most fixes happen inside the tank, with cheap parts and no special tools.
need: Food coloring or a toilet dye tablet
An old towel (to set the tank lid on)
Your phone, to photograph the old flapper
A replacement flapper that matches your toilet (if needed)
before: Before you replace any parts, close the toilet's shutoff valve by turning it clockwise, then flush to empty the tank.

steps.how: Lift off the tank lid and set it on a towel. Put a few drops of food coloring in the tank. Don't flush. Wait at least 10 minutes. If color shows up in the bowl, water is leaking past the flapper.
Flush right after the test so the dye doesn't stain the tank.
Watch the tank refill. If water keeps spilling into the tall open tube in the middle (the overflow tube), the water level is set too high.

The water should stop about 1/2 to 1 inch below the top of the overflow tube. For a ball on an arm, turn the adjusting screw where the arm meets the fill valve. For a float that slides on the fill valve, squeeze its clip and slide it down. Flush and check again.
The chain from the handle to the flapper should be neither too short nor too long. Too short, and it holds the flapper open; too long, and it can tangle or get caught under the flapper.
If you have to jiggle the handle to stop the running, tighten the nut that holds the handle to the tank. If that doesn't help, the handle may need replacing.

Turn off the water and flush to empty the tank. Unhook the old flapper and take it, or a photo of it, to the store to find a match. Hook on the new one, attach the chain about as it was, turn the water back on, and flush to test.
Repeat the dye test to make sure the leak is gone.

pro: If the toilet keeps running or won't flush after these fixes, contact a local plumber.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Floats, valves, and the siphon
body: The tank stores water for the next flush. When you push the handle, a lever lifts the flapper, and tank water rushes into the bowl.

The bowl drains through a curved pipe called the trapway. The rush of water fills it and pushes out the air, and that change in pressure starts a siphon. The siphon pulls water and waste down the drain until air gets back in and breaks it, which is the gurgle at the end of a flush.

As the tank empties, the float drops and opens the fill valve. Water pours in and the float rises with it. It floats because water pushes up on it with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside. At the set level, the rising float shuts the valve.

If the flapper doesn't seal, water trickles into the bowl, the tank level slowly drops, and the fill valve turns on again by itself. That's why a worn flapper can make a toilet seem to flush or refill on its own.
how_it_works.formula: buoyant force = weight of the water the float pushes aside
how_it_works.try: Push an empty, capped plastic bottle down into a sink full of water. Feel it push back. The deeper you push, the more water it moves aside and the harder it pushes up, until it's all the way under.

teach: Let your child do the dye test. It feels like a science experiment.
Flush with the tank lid off so they can watch the flapper, chain, float, and fill valve move in order.
Leak math: EPA says an average home's leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons a year. Divide by 365 to find about how many gallons a day that is (about 25).
Bring them along to the hardware store to match the flapper.
tips: Do the dye test at least once a year.
EPA WaterSense suggests replacing the flapper at least every five years.
When buying a flapper, check its width and whether it has a foam float. Take the old one or a photo with you.
Mark the water line in the tank with a pencil before you adjust the float, so you can compare.

mistakes.problem: Chain too tight, so the flapper never fully closes.
mistakes.fix: Leave a little slack so the chain rests without lifting the flapper.

mistakes.problem: Chain too long, so it gets caught under the flapper.
mistakes.fix: Hook it to a different link to shorten it.

mistakes.problem: Water level set too high, so water trickles down the overflow tube.
mistakes.fix: Lower the float until the water stops about 1/2 to 1 inch below the top of the tube.

mistakes.problem: Buying a flapper that doesn't match.
mistakes.fix: Take the old flapper or a photo to the store and match it.

guides.name: Unclog a Sink or Toilet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 9, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Clogs happen in every home. A plunger clears most sink and toilet clogs in a few minutes, with no chemicals. Knowing which plunger to grab, how to get a good seal, and when to stop saves a mess and sometimes a service call.
need: Cup plunger (a plain rubber cup) for sinks, tubs, and showers
Flange plunger (a cup with an extra rubber sleeve) for toilets
before: If the toilet bowl is full and not draining, don't flush again. It can overflow.
If someone has already poured a chemical drain cleaner into the drain, don't plunge it and don't add any other product. Call a plumber.

steps.how: Use a cup plunger for sinks, tubs, and showers. Use a flange plunger, with its extra rubber lip, for toilets. It seals better in the toilet's drain.
For a sink, stuff a wet rag into the overflow hole near the rim. For a double sink, plug the other drain. This keeps your push aimed at the clog.
You need enough water to cover the plunger's cup so it can seal. If a toilet bowl is very full, scoop some water into a bucket first.
Set the plunger over the drain so the cup covers the opening completely.
Press down smoothly, then pull up sharply. Repeat 20 to 30 times without breaking the seal. In a toilet, use quick, strong strokes.
Lift the plunger and watch. If the water drains, run water to rinse the sink. Flush a toilet only once its bowl drains normally. If it doesn't drain, try another round.
If plunging fails, a hand drain snake can reach farther. Feed the cable into the drain and crank the handle until you feel resistance. Turn it to hook or break up the clog, then pull it out.
If the clog still won't clear, call a plumber.

pro: If plunging and a hand snake don't clear the clog, call a plumber.
If water backs up in more than one place, like a toilet or shower when the washing machine drains, the blockage may be farther down the line. Call a plumber.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why a plunger works
body: Pressure is force spread over an area. When you push a plunger down, your force presses on the water trapped under the cup.

Water is very close to incompressible, which means it barely squeezes smaller. Instead of shrinking, it passes the push along. Pascal's principle says a change in pressure in one part of a fluid travels through all of it. So your push travels down the pipe to the clog. Pulling up sharply tugs the other way, rocking the clog back and forth until it breaks loose.
That's why the seal and the water matter. Air squeezes easily, so a cup full of air just squishes. And if the overflow hole is open, the push escapes out of it instead of reaching the clog.
how_it_works.try: Fill a plastic bottle to the very top with water, cap it, and squeeze. Then pour out half, cap it again, and squeeze. The half-full bottle squishes easily because air compresses. The full one pushes back because water doesn't.

teach: Show your child the two plungers and let them pick the right one for each job.
Practice on a slow sink first. It's less messy than a toilet.
Talk about what never goes down a toilet: dental floss, hair, gum, and anything that isn't toilet paper.
Keep a plunger near each toilet so no one has to hunt for one in a hurry.
tips: Keep a cover or strainer over sink and tub drains to catch hair and food bits.
Never pour grease down a drain. Let it cool in a can, then put it in the trash.
Clean hair out of the tub drain after washing your hair.
Wear rubber gloves and lay an old towel around the base. It can get messy.

mistakes.problem: Flushing a clogged toilet again to 'push it through'.
mistakes.fix: Don't. If the water is high and not draining, another flush can overflow the bowl. Plunge instead.

mistakes.problem: Using a cup plunger on a toilet.
mistakes.fix: Use a flange plunger. Its rubber sleeve seals in the toilet's drain.

mistakes.problem: Plunging a sink with the overflow hole open.
mistakes.fix: Plug the overflow with a wet rag so the pressure goes toward the clog.

mistakes.problem: Mixing drain cleaners, or plunging after using one.
mistakes.fix: Never mix products, and never plunge a drain that has chemical cleaner in it. Call a plumber.

safety: Never mix drain cleaners or other cleaning products. They can react and give off dangerous fumes.
Don't use a plunger on a drain with chemical drain cleaner in it.

guides.name: Change a Furnace Air Filter
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Most homes with central heating or air conditioning have an air filter that catches dust before air runs through the system. A clogged filter blocks airflow, wastes energy, and can let dirt reach parts that are hard to clean. Changing it is one of the easiest home jobs there is.
need: A new filter in the exact size printed on the old one
Screwdriver, if the filter cover has screws
Step stool or ladder, if the filter is up high or in the attic
before: Turn the heating and cooling system off at the thermostat.

steps.how: Go to the furnace or air handler, which may be in a utility room, basement, closet, attic, crawl space, or garage. The filter usually slides into a slot between the return duct and the unit. In some homes it sits behind a return-air grille in a wall or ceiling instead.
Switch the system off at the thermostat before you open anything.
Open the cover (it may have screws, clips, or a latch) and slide the filter out. Handle it carefully; the wire on some filters can be sharp.
The length, width, and thickness are printed on the cardboard frame. Buy that exact size. It should cover the opening and fit snugly without bending.
Look for the airflow arrow on the new filter's frame. Point it into the duct, toward the furnace, the way the air moves.
Take off the plastic wrap (not the cardboard frame) and write today's date where you'll see it next time.

steps.t: Slide it in and close up
steps.how: Slide the filter into the slot, arrow toward the furnace. Put the cover back on. Don't tape it shut, since you'll open it again.
Set the thermostat back to normal. Put a reminder on the calendar for the next check.

pro: Before switching to a MERV 13 or higher filter, ask an HVAC technician or your service company whether your system can handle it.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: How a filter catches dust
body: A fan in the system pulls air from your rooms through the return duct, pushes it through the filter, heats or cools it, and sends it back out. The filter is a mat of fibers. Air slips through the gaps, while many particles, like dust and pollen, get caught.

MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It's a number for comparing filters: the higher the MERV, the better the filter is at trapping small particles. But a filter that catches more can also clog faster and slow the airflow, so your system has to be able to handle it.

As a filter fills up, air has a harder time getting through. That lowers the system's efficiency, and some dirty air can sneak around the filter onto the cooling coil. Energy.gov says replacing a dirty, clogged filter can cut an air conditioner's energy use by 5% to 15%. One more fact: a filter only cleans the air while the system is running.
how_it_works.formula: energy saved ≈ cooling energy cost × 0.05 to 0.15 (5% to 15%)
how_it_works.try: Hold the new filter and the old one up to a lamp. Which lets more light through? Then do the math: if cooling costs $100 a month, a clean filter could save about 5% to 15%, or $5 to $15.

teach: Let your child read the size off the old filter and find the match at the store.
Make the arrow rule a chant: 'Arrow points to the furnace.'
Hold the old and new filters side by side so they can see what the filter caught.
Let them write the date on the new filter.
tips: How often depends on your filter and system, so follow the maker's directions. EPA says many makers suggest every 60 to 90 days. Energy.gov suggests every month or two during cooling season.
Check more often if you have pets, a dusty home, or the system runs constantly.
If the old filter looks very dirty when you change it, change it more often.
If your slot fits more than one thickness, the thicker filter has more surface area for catching dust.
Buy a few filters at a time so you always have a spare.

mistakes.problem: Putting the filter in backward.
mistakes.fix: Point the arrow into the duct, toward the furnace.

mistakes.problem: Buying a filter that's 'close enough' in size.
mistakes.fix: Match all three numbers on the frame. It should cover the opening and fit snugly without bending.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting when you last changed it.
mistakes.fix: Write the date on the frame and set a calendar reminder.

mistakes.problem: Jumping to the highest MERV without checking.
mistakes.fix: Ask an HVAC pro whether your system can handle it.

safety: Turn the system off at the thermostat before you pull the filter.
Handle filters carefully. The wire on some can be sharp.
Use a ladder if the filter is in the attic.

guides.name: Test Smoke and CO Alarms
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help from about 8, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms are some of the cheapest life-savers in a home, but only if they work. Testing them takes a few minutes a month. Knowing their age, where they belong, and what to do when one sounds matters just as much.
need: A sturdy step stool or ladder
Replacement batteries of the type printed on each alarm
A helper to steady the ladder
before: Read the instructions for each alarm. Mounting, testing, and replacement details can vary by model.

steps.how: Walk through the house and list each alarm. Smoke alarms belong inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level of the home, including the basement.
Push each smoke alarm's test button. It should sound loudly. Do this once a month.
If an alarm doesn't sound, put in a new battery and test again. If it still doesn't sound, replace the alarm.
Look on the back for the date it was made. Replace any smoke alarm that is 10 years old or older, even if it still beeps.
If your alarms use replaceable batteries, change them at least once a year. Sealed 10-year alarms don't get new batteries; you replace the whole alarm when its time is up.
Test CO alarms monthly. They belong outside sleeping areas and on every level of the home. Check the manual for when to replace them.
A chirp from a smoke alarm usually means its battery is low; replace the battery right away. A loud, steady alarm means danger.
If the CO alarm sounds, everyone goes outside to fresh air right away, then you call 911. Nobody goes back in until emergency responders say it's safe.

pro: Hardwired alarms, the kind wired into the house, should be installed by a qualified electrician.
If a CO alarm went off and you suspect an appliance, don't use that appliance again until trained service personnel have checked it.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Two ways to sense smoke, and one gas you can't
body: Ionization alarms hold a tiny, safely shielded amount of radioactive material. It lets the air between two metal plates carry a small electric current. When smoke drifts in, the particles grab the charged bits of air and carry them away, so the current drops. When it drops enough, the alarm sounds. These respond faster to fast, flaming fires.

Photoelectric alarms shine a light beam through a dark chamber, aimed so it misses a light sensor. When smoke drifts in, the particles scatter the light, and some of it bounces onto the sensor. These respond faster to slow, smoldering fires. Because no one knows what kind of fire might start, safety agencies recommend having both kinds, or dual-sensor alarms.
Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no color and no smell. Your nose can't warn you, so a CO alarm has to.
how_it_works.formula: replace-by year for a smoke alarm = year it was made + 10
how_it_works.try: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through the side of a clear glass of water. Then stir in a few drops of milk. Now you can see the beam, because the tiny milk droplets scatter the light. A photoelectric alarm uses the same idea with smoke.

teach: Let your child press the test button while a grown-up steadies the ladder, so they know the sound.
Teach the difference: a chirp means 'change my battery'; a loud, steady alarm means 'get out'.
Make a chart of every alarm, where it is, and its replace-by year.
Practice the CO plan: outside first, then call 911.
tips: Pick an easy date for battery changes, like when you change your clocks.
Interconnected alarms are best: when one sounds, they all sound.
Mount smoke alarms on the ceiling or high on a wall, following the instructions. CPSC says wall alarms go about 6 to 12 inches below the ceiling.
If cooking sets off an alarm, open a window, press the hush button, or wave a towel. Never take out the battery.
A CO alarm's test button checks its circuits, not the accuracy of its sensor, so replace it on time.
There are alarms with strobe lights or vibration for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

mistakes.problem: Pulling the battery because cooking keeps setting off the alarm.
mistakes.fix: Use the hush button, or move the alarm a few feet farther from the kitchen. Disabling an alarm can be a deadly mistake.

mistakes.problem: Keeping an old smoke alarm because it still beeps.
mistakes.fix: Replace smoke alarms 10 years from the date they were made.

mistakes.problem: Having alarms only in hallways.
mistakes.fix: Add one inside each bedroom too, and on every level.

mistakes.problem: Ignoring a CO alarm because nobody smells anything.
mistakes.fix: CO has no smell. Treat every CO alarm as real: go outside, then call 911.

safety: If the CO alarm sounds, move everyone outside to fresh air right away, then call 911.
Stay out until emergency responders say it's safe to go back in.
Never disable a smoke alarm or take out its battery.

guides.name: Find a Stud and Hang a Picture
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Hanging a picture well means it sits level and stays on the wall. Behind most walls are wooden posts called studs, and a hook or screw that reaches a stud holds much better than one in drywall alone. When there's no stud where you need one, a wall anchor rated for the weight does the job.
need: Wall anchors rated for your picture's weight (if there's no stud)
Hammer, and a drill or screwdriver
before: Pick a spot where a heavy frame or mirror won't hang over a bed, couch, or chair, in case it ever falls.

steps.how: Have a helper hold the picture up while you step back. Lightly mark the top center with a pencil.

Slide a stud finder sideways along the wall and mark where it signals. Mark the middle of the stud, not its edge. Studs run from floor to ceiling and are usually 16 or 24 inches apart, so once you find one, measure over to check for the next.
Try pushing a thumbtack into the wall. If it won't break the surface, the wall is probably plaster rather than drywall.
Pull the picture's wire up tight, the way it will hang, and measure from the wire to the top of the frame. Your hook goes that far below where you want the top of the frame.

steps.t: Use the stud if you can
steps.how: Use a hook or screw long enough to go through the drywall and into the stud. For large pictures, FEMA suggests eye-hooks at least 1 to 2 inches long. You should feel steady resistance the whole way in; if it suddenly goes easy, you've probably missed the stud.

steps.t: Use an anchor if there's no stud
steps.how: Pick an anchor whose package says it holds more than your picture weighs. Drill the hole size the package lists, tap the anchor in until it's flush, then drive in the screw.

steps.t: Use two hooks for big frames
steps.how: Large pictures and mirrors are steadier on two hooks than on one. Space them evenly from the center.
Hang the picture, set the bubble level on top of the frame, and nudge it until the bubble sits between the lines.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: Spacing, measuring, and the bubble
body: Studs are usually spaced 16 or 24 inches apart. Builders measure that spacing from the center of one stud to the center of the next, called 'on center.' If you find a stud center 30 inches from a corner and the spacing is 16 inches, the next ones are likely near 46 and 62 inches. The pattern helps you guess, and the stud finder confirms.

Hanging height is subtraction. If you want the top of the frame at 64 inches and the tight wire sits 4 inches below the top, the hook goes at 64 − 4 = 60 inches. To center a picture on a wall, divide the wall's width by 2.

A bubble level is a small tube of liquid with an air bubble inside. Air is less dense than the liquid, so the liquid pushes the bubble up to the highest spot. The tube bulges slightly in the middle, so when the level is perfectly flat, the highest spot is the center, and the bubble rests between the lines.
how_it_works.formula: hook height = height you want for the top of the frame − distance from the tight wire to the top
how_it_works.try: Tilt a capped water bottle with a little air in it and watch the bubble race to the higher end. Lay it on a table, then slowly raise one end with a book and watch the bubble move.

teach: Let your child run the stud finder and mark each signal with painter's tape.
Have them do the hook-height math on paper before anyone makes a hole.
Make them the 'level reader' who calls out 'left side up' or 'right side up'.
tips: Painter's tape lets you mark the wall without pencil smudges.
Check the anchor package for the weight it holds and the drill bit size it needs.
Skip patched or water-damaged drywall. Anchors can slip out of it.
Nails or hooks that go only into drywall or plaster are less secure than ones that reach a stud.

mistakes.problem: Hanging a heavy frame from drywall alone.
mistakes.fix: Use a stud, or an anchor rated for more than the frame weighs.

mistakes.problem: The screw suddenly goes in easily partway.
mistakes.fix: You've probably missed the stud. Find its center again, or switch to an anchor.

mistakes.problem: Measuring to the wire while it hangs loose.
mistakes.fix: Pull the wire up tight, the way it sits on the hook, before you measure.

mistakes.problem: Hanging a big mirror over the bed or couch.
mistakes.fix: Choose a spot where a fall couldn't land on anyone.

safety: Don't hang large pictures or mirrors over beds, couches, or chairs.
Use hardware rated for the weight. Check the package.

guides.name: Patch a Small Hole in Drywall
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Nail holes, small dents, and dings show up in every home. For holes smaller than about 1/2 inch, a little spackle and a putty knife make them disappear. It's a good first repair, because a mistake can be sanded off and tried again.
need: Fine sanding sponge or fine sandpaper

steps.how: This method is for small holes, under about 1/2 inch across. Bigger holes need a patch and joint compound.
Brush away loose bits and wipe off dust so the spackle sticks.
Scoop a little spackle onto the tip of the putty knife. Press it into the hole, then pull the knife across the wall to smooth it.
Spread the edges thin so they blend into the wall. After two or three strokes, stop and leave it alone.
Wait until it's completely dry. Small spots can dry quickly, but check the container for the time.
Sand gently with a fine sanding sponge until the patch is smooth and even with the wall.

steps.t: Add a second coat if needed
steps.how: Spackle shrinks a little as it dries, so a small dip may show. Add a thin second coat, let it dry, and sand again.
Prime the patch, then paint it to match. Without primer, the patch can look shinier or duller than the wall around it.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: What drywall is made of
body: Drywall is a sheet of gypsum pressed between two layers of heavy paper. Gypsum is a mineral, and most of the gypsum used in the United States goes into wallboard for homes and other buildings.

Chemically, gypsum is calcium sulfate dihydrate, written CaSO4·2H2O. 'Dihydrate' means two water molecules are locked into each unit of the crystal. That built-in water is about 20 percent of gypsum's weight, and it's part of why drywall resists fire: it takes a lot of heat to drive that water out.
Spackle from a tub is a paste with water in it. As the water evaporates, the paste dries, hardens, and shrinks a little. That's why a deep fill can sink and need a second thin coat.
how_it_works.formula: gypsum = CaSO4·2H2O (calcium sulfate with 2 water molecules)
how_it_works.try: Spread a thin smear and a thick blob of spackle on a scrap of cardboard. Check them every 15 minutes. Which one dries first? Does the thick one shrink or crack as it dries?

teach: Let your child fill old nail holes. Sanding fixes almost any mistake.
Teach 'less is more': thin coats and just a few strokes.
After painting, compare a primed patch with an unprimed one so they can see why primer matters.
tips: Fill the hole just slightly proud of the wall, since spackle shrinks as it dries.
Thin coats dry faster and sand more easily than one thick coat.
Prime and paint a whole section of wall if you want the color and shine to match evenly.
Keep leftover wall paint labeled with the room name for future touch-ups.

mistakes.problem: Sanding before the spackle is completely dry.
mistakes.fix: Wait the full drying time on the container.

mistakes.problem: Piling on one thick blob.
mistakes.fix: Use thin layers and let each one dry before the next.

mistakes.problem: Skipping primer.
mistakes.fix: Prime the patch so the paint's shine matches the rest of the wall.

mistakes.problem: Using spackle alone on a big hole.
mistakes.fix: Holes larger than about 1/2 inch need a patch and joint compound.

safety: If your home was built before 1978, its paint may contain lead. Sanding or scraping lead paint makes dust that is harmful, especially to children, so learn the lead-safe steps from EPA before you sand old paint.
